summary: Defines SDP semantics for signaling that one media description depends on others for decoding, which is needed when layered or multiple-description coded media is split across different network streams. A receiver can then know which streams to combine.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a puzzle sent in several envelopes. This adds a note saying which envelopes must be opened together before the picture makes sense.

questions: what is the sdp depend attribute
what is ddp grouping in sdp
how does sdp signal layered video dependency
what is an operation point in layered coding
subtitle: How SDP tells a receiver which media streams must be decoded together when layered or multi-description video is split across streams.

tldr.problem: When a layered or multiple description coded media stream is split into separate RTP streams, SDP cannot say how those streams depend on each other, so a receiver cannot tell which ones to pick.
tldr.mechanism: A new grouping type DDP, used with the mid attribute from RFC 3388, collects the media descriptions, and a new media-level attribute depend names which format in which other media description each format needs.
tldr.outcome: A receiver or middle box can work out the valid Operation Points from the SDP alone. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 5583 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2009. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Missing Dependency Signal
sections.content:
An SDP session description can hold several media descriptions, each starting with an m= line. Today, if several m= lines have the same media type, a receiver cannot tell how they relate to each other.

That is a problem for layered and Multiple Description Coding (MDC) media. These codings produce Media Partitions that are each sent in their own media stream. Senders, network elements or receivers can drop some partitions and still get a worse but useful picture. RFC 5583 adds an SDP extension that states the decoding dependency between such streams.

The trigger was work on an RTP payload format for Scalable Video Coding (SVC), but the memo is generic. The mechanisms apply only together with RTP (RFC 3550). Grouping media lines of different media types is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes one video is cut into pieces and mailed in separate envelopes. SDP had no way to say which envelopes belong together, and this fixes that.

sections.title: Partitions, Dependencies and Operation Points
sections.content:
A Media Bitstream is a valid, decodable stream with all the partitions the encoder made. A Media Partition is a subset meant to travel on its own. In layered coding a partition is one or more layers handled as a unit. In MDC it is one or more descriptions.

A decoding dependency is the kind of relationship partitions have. Two are defined. In layered dependency, each partition is only decodable when all partitions it depends on are available, so the dependencies form a directed graph. In MDC dependency, N of M partitions are required to form a Media Bitstream, with no hierarchy between them.

An Operation Point is a subset of the bitstream that includes every partition needed to reconstruct at a certain quality or other property, and no others. Every media stream in a group must contain at least one Operation Point.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a layer cake. The top layer cannot stand without the ones below it, and an Operation Point is a slice that has every layer it needs.

sections.title: Why Plain SDP Is Not Enough
sections.content:
Layered and MDC coding share one goal: adapting media to network conditions such as bandwidth, error rates and the connectivity of endpoints in multicast or broadcast. A classic use is receiver-driven layered multicast, where a receiver picks a combination of streams to match its quality or bit-rate needs.

Older layered codecs had a one-dimensional hierarchy: each enhancement layer referred to exactly one layer below it. SDP supports exactly that by letting a media description carry a range of transport addresses, where a higher address means a higher layer. Newer formats, including Multi-View Coding, allow at least tree-shaped dependency hierarchies, which SDP could not express. Without that, receivers cannot make an informed choice about which layers to subscribe to.

The RFC also describes sending different layers over transmission paths with different cost, protection or quality of service. For example, a base layer can go over high QoS or serve as an unencrypted free preview, while an encrypted enhancement layer references it.
sections.plainLanguage: Old SDP could only say 'each piece sits on the one below it'. New video formats build more tangled stacks, and SDP had no way to describe them.

sections.title: The DDP Group and the depend Attribute
sections.content:
The new grouping semantic DDP (Decoding Dependency) builds on the mid attribute from RFC 3388. All media descriptions in a DDP group MUST have the same media type and the same type of decoding dependency. A media description MUST NOT be part of more than one DDP group. If several codecs are offered, the media streams MUST have the same dependency structure whichever payload type is used.

The new media-level attribute depend lists, for each dependent format (an RTP payload type), a dependency type and the formats it relies on, each tagged with the mid of the media description it lives in. There MUST be exactly one dependency tag per dependent format. If a list of formats is given for one media description, any one element satisfies the dependency, at the choice of the decoder.

Two dependency types are defined. With lay, all streams needed to decode the Operation Point MUST be named. With mdc, at least N of the M streams of the group are needed to form an Operation Point, but N and M are not signaled. New dependency types MUST be defined in a Standards-Track document.
sections.plainLanguage: Each piece gets a sticky note: 'I only work if you also have piece 96 or 97 from envelope L1'. The word lay or mdc says what kind of note it is.

sections.title: Offer/Answer and Declarative Use
sections.content:
A node that does not understand DDP grouping SHOULD either answer while ignoring the grouping or refuse the offer (for example with 488 or 606 in SIP). If the offerer still wants a session, it SHOULD send a new offer with a single media stream that represents one Operation Point, usually the base layer.

If the answerer understands DDP, the offerer decides the number of media streams and the dependencies between them, and the answerer cannot change those relations. For unicast media that the answerer receives, it MAY remove Operation Points. It MUST use the offered dependency relations when it sends. For multicast, the answerer MUST either accept all Operation Points or remove the non-accepted ones completely. If it cannot accept something, it MAY re-invite with an acceptable offer.

In declarative use such as RTSP, a receiver that understands this signaling SHALL set up all media streams needed to decode its chosen Operation Point. One that does not falls back to normal SDP processing. The mechanism MUST NOT be used to negotiate between the AVP and SAVP RTP profiles, though both may be used with it. Interaction with capability negotiation is left for further study.
sections.plainLanguage: The person who makes the offer decides how the puzzle is cut up. The other side can say 'I will skip some pieces', but it cannot change which pieces need which.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The layered example has three video media descriptions, L1, L2 and L3, grouped with a=group:DDP L1 L2 L3. L1 carries H264 payload types 96 and 97 and is the base layer. Payload type 100 in L3 depends on 96 or 97 in L1, which is an exclusive choice: one of the two is required. Payload type 101 depends on 97 in L1 and also on 99 in L2, and both are required.

The MDC example has three media descriptions M1, M2 and M3 with one format each (104, 105 and 106). Each lists the other two with mdc. In that case the other formats can be used to enhance decoding, but they are not required for it.
sections.plainLanguage: In the cake example the top slice needs a specific lower slice. In the MDC example every piece is useful alone and gets better when friends join it.

sections.title: Security and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
All security implications of SDP apply. An attacker who changes the dependency signaling could mislead a receiver or middle box into combining RTP streams that do not form a valid Operation Point, with potentially fatal consequences for decoding. Receivers SHOULD check the integrity of the SDP and follow the SDP security considerations, trusting SDP only from trusted sources.

IANA registered the group semantics token DDP and the media-level attribute depend (long form: decoding dependency), plus the two attribute values lay and mdc. New values for depend are added under the Specification Required policy.
sections.plainLanguage: If a trickster edits the notes, you might glue together pieces that do not fit. So you should only trust notes from someone you trust.

viz.caption: THE DEPEND LINES OF THE LAYERED EXAMPLE (RFC 5583)

data.title: Layered dependency example
data.code:
a=group:DDP L1 L2 L3
m=video 40000 RTP/AVP 96 97
a=mid:L1
m=video 40002 RTP/AVP 98 99
a=mid:L2
a=depend:98 lay L1:96,97; 99 lay L1:97
m=video 40004 RTP/AVP 100 101
a=mid:L3
a=depend:100 lay L1:96,97; 101 lay L1:97 L2:99

viz.caption: DEPENDENCY TYPES REGISTERED FOR THE DEPEND ATTRIBUTE

items.label: Layered decoding dependency
items.desc: Streams are layers; each needs the ones it depends on.

items.label: Multi-descriptive decoding dependency
items.desc: At least N of M streams are needed; no hierarchy between them.
